title: Fungal infection reduces thermal breadth and induces metabolic depression under warm conditions in an endangered amphibian
content:

Abstract

Climate change and infectious disease are pervasive ecological stressors that can interact to reshape organismal physiology. While temperature governs both host and pathogen performance, infection can also alter host physiological functioning across thermal environments. Thus, quantifying how infection shapes the thermal physiological traits that impact fitness in changing environments can improve predictions of the effects of endemic disease and rising temperatures on threatened populations. Global amphibian populations have experienced severe declines due to chytridiomycosis, a disease caused by the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), and recent work suggests that climate change may worsen disease outbreaks. Bd has had devastating impacts on the Panamanian golden frog (Atelopus zeteki), which experienced severe population declines in the early 2000s, and subsequent captive breeding programs were established with the goal of eventual reintroduction. To understand the role of temperature and disease on the future resilience of this species, we examined the influence of acclimation temperature (17°C and 25°C) and Bd infection on A. zeteki physiology using a full before-after-control-impact (BACI) experimental design, using frogs derived from two source populations. We quantified critical thermal limits (CTmax and CTmin), the thermal sensitivity of jumping performance and resting metabolic rate (RMR) before and after Bd exposure. Thermal acclimation shifted baseline thermal limits, with warm-acclimated frogs exhibiting higher CTmax and CTmin than cool-acclimated frogs. Bd infection was the strongest predictor of mortality and reduced CTmax in a load-dependent manner, with the timing of decline dependent on acclimation history (earlier at 17°C and delayed at 25°C). Jumping performance increased with test temperature and differed between source populations but was not reduced by Bd infection. Bd-infected frogs had depressed metabolic rates at warmer test temperatures, indicating temperature-dependent metabolic disruption during infection. Together, these results provide mechanistic insight that can help refine captive breeding protocols and guide the selection of release environments for Bd-susceptible amphibians under climate warming. More broadly, our results reveal that pathogen infection can constrain thermal tolerance and disrupt metabolic function in a temperature-dependent manner, highlighting a mechanism by which disease may exacerbate organismal vulnerability under ongoing climate warming.
